Lack of project management experience.

Independent developer here as well and the first thing you quickly learn is to try and take your absolute best guess at how long something might take you. Give yourself a pretty healthy buffer and then finally multiply it all by 10 and you have a realistic, if not tight, time frame. By the time you've really got things down, you might be able to get it down to 2-3x or so. but even when allowing yourself a buffer, there will inevitably be unforeseen obstacles and more than you expected. Of course this isn't unique to independent developers. The reason 'crunch' in professional development exists is because of this phenomena. It's also the reason that even though companies like Ubisoft or Activision basically produce their games on a factory line at this point, they invariably launch with mountains of bugs. They can't meet their deadline so they just rush to it out and we get whatever their latest 'kinda stable' build is when the production deadline hits.

Kickstarters tend to lay out lengthy timelines which are going to be insufficient and the developers may be reaching above their technical capacity in many instances. There's also the issue that the more you work on a project, the less interesting it becomes. When you've already funded the developer in whole, you better hope they've got a whole heck of a lot of self discipline and ethics because they're going to be working day in-day out on something that they've likely already obtained a very healthy chunk of the potential revenue for and they're probably not longer particularly enjoying doing.
